name: Grace Costa

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers, AI companies, unions, parties or government. Your answers stay confidential. Could you walk me through an ordinary shift?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I lead the loading shift at a large copper mine. I operate the shovel when someone is away, but much of my day is checking benches, coaching new operators and deciding when a truck should stop. My two-year technical diploma got me in; twenty years of watching rock move made me good at it. My partner Eva works at a school, our two children are at school too, and we have a mortgage and about nine months of expenses saved. I sometimes use AI to tidy a shift report after I have written the facts myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew a little faster paperwork is welcome if operators still sign off on safety calls. A neat report cannot certify a stable mine bench.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my job stays much the same, though the company may ask why we need as many people on reporting. Eva's school pay and our nine-month cushion mean I can argue for the trainees without fearing next month's mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep the weekly bench walk with the new operators and check any computer-drafted report against my notebook. During the first year, I'll raise any missing hazard notes at our joint safety meeting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steady, with a bit of irritation at the idea that typing was the hard part. The hard part is telling a young operator to stop a loaded truck.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which call would still need a person on site?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last winter a hairline crack opened along the south bench after rain. I marked it before the morning truck run, and I'd make the same stop call regardless of what a screen said.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your household cushion change what you say at work?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Eva that our savings let me speak up, but I know not everyone on my crew has that room. I wouldn't spend the cushion just because this card sounds mild.

say: I would welcome **quicker reports** if operators still sign off on every safety decision.
I would tell the crew a **neat document** cannot certify a stable bench.
think: I expect my **lead role** to stay, though routine reporting may need fewer hands.
I can defend **trainees** because Eva earns and our nine months of savings give our household room.
do: **Keep walking** the benches weekly with new operators and check computer drafts against my notebook.
**Raise missing hazards** in the joint safety meeting during the first year.
feel: **Steady**, with irritation when paperwork is mistaken for the hard part of mining.
S0.quote: A neat report cannot certify a stable mine bench.
fieldNote: Her **safety judgment** comes from cracks and traffic on an actual bench, not polished report text.
A **nine-month cushion** and second household wage support her willingness to defend trainees publicly.

steps.text: Keep weekly bench walks with new operators
Raise omitted hazard notes in the joint safety meeting

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say dispatch, purchasing and shift reports may change before any machine replaces a shovel operator. Our safety committee should see the route rules before software starts setting truck loads.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think management might use faster planning to squeeze the gaps between trucks. My lead post is secure for now, but a faster schedule could leave the least experienced drivers with less room for mistakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask to sit with dispatch while they trial the planning tool, and I'll compare its routes with our incident book. In the first year, I'll bring the operators' written concerns to the joint safety committee before any new target becomes a shift rule.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alert rather than frightened for my own wage. I picture a new driver facing a screen that says the road is clear after heavy rain.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you stop a software route?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd stop the run if a route crossed the south bench after a fresh crack. The software can be corrected; a loaded truck cannot be pulled back from a slip.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you want in the planning trial?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The dispatch clerk might lose tasks first, so I'd ask whether that person can help check exceptions. I don't want safety oversight quietly cut while the mine celebrates a quicker schedule.

say: I would expect **dispatch and purchasing** to change before shovel operation.
I would ask the **safety committee** to inspect route rules before software sets truck loads.
think: I worry that **faster schedules** could leave new drivers less time to judge a bad road.
I expect my **lead wage** to hold, but safety oversight could shrink without open review.
do: **Sit with dispatch** during the planning trial and compare routes with the incident book.
**Take concerns** from operators to the joint safety committee before targets become shift rules.
feel: **Alert** for newer drivers, while feeling secure in her own post and income.
S1.quote: The software can be corrected; a loaded truck cannot be pulled back from a slip.
fieldNote: She focuses on **route rules** and truck spacing, which are plausible early effects of thinking AI.
Her **public action** uses the joint safety committee; she does not claim that robots already run the shovel.

steps.text: Test planning routes with dispatch against the incident book
Bring operator concerns to the joint safety committee

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say full thinking AI by 2028 could remake dispatch while people still run the big machines until capable robots arrive around 2031. I want the union and mine to publish a paid transition agreement before anyone loses a roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think my lead experience buys me some time, and nine months of savings gives us options. Yet I cannot promise every trainee a safety job when the trucks and shovels eventually need fewer drivers.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Starting this winter I'll ask the union to bargain for paid equipment-inspection training and clear selection rules. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'll take the inspection training if places and full wages are guaranteed; meanwhile I'll keep leading the shift.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel responsible and uneasy, not without choices. My own mortgage is covered for a while, but I know which apprentices have no such cushion.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make a training agreement usable?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would put the agreement's wage and places on the notice board, not just a cheerful promise about retraining. A parent on rotating shifts cannot live on an unpaid course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does your savings cushion make you less likely to act?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell Eva that the nine months are for our family, not a reason to stay quiet. I'd spend union meeting time now because the robot date is closer than the children finishing school.

say: I would tell the crew **thinking AI** reaches dispatch in 2028, before capable mine robots around 2031.
I would demand a **paid transition** with clear selection rules before driving and shovel rosters disappear.
think: I have **nine months saved** and a senior role, but I cannot promise each trainee a replacement job.
I worry most about **apprentices** with no cushion if the mine eventually needs fewer operators.
do: **Ask the union** this winter to bargain for paid inspection training and published selection rules.
**Take inspection training** after thinking AI arrives if places and full wages are guaranteed.
feel: **Uneasy** about trainees, while her own savings and senior role leave her choices.
S2.quote: A parent on rotating shifts cannot live on an unpaid course.
fieldNote: She separates **2028 thinking work** from capable robots reaching mine equipment around 2031.
Her training plan is **conditional** on a funded place and full wages; she does not assume a job is reserved.

steps.text: Ask the union to bargain for paid inspection training
Take inspection training if a place and full wages are guaranteed

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years to thinking AI in 2031 and robots around 2034 is enough to negotiate in the open. We should trial new equipment under crew supervision before anyone signs away a driving roster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I could move into site safety inspection, but I would need the credential and an actual vacancy. I'm 43 now; at about 51 when robots arrive, I'd rather build on my mining years than start over somewhere else.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll ask the union education officer this year which inspection certificate counts at our mine. If the mine funds a place, I'll enroll next year, then apply for a posted site-safety opening in the first year after thinking AI arrives.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel more hopeful with a proper runway. That hope depends on the mine being willing to pay for real instruction, not just a video and a badge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need before enrolling?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would still walk the benches during the course, because hazards look different after a blast. A certificate cannot replace watching the ground move.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What if the inspection job does not exist?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If no site-safety vacancy opens, I'd stay leading the loading shift and keep pushing for operator representation on equipment trials. We have plenty of nearby mines, but I won't move the family for a rumour.

say: I would use the **five-year window** to negotiate supervised trials before capable robots arrive around 2034.
I would insist a **real certificate** and posted safety vacancies sit behind transition promises.
think: I could use my **mining experience** in inspection if an actual vacancy and credential exist.
I would be about **51** when robots arrive, so a related role suits me better than a fresh career.
do: **Check certificate rules** with the union education officer this year.
**Enroll next year** if the mine funds a place, then apply for a posted site-safety opening after thinking AI arrives.
feel: **Hopeful** with time to prepare, contingent on funded instruction and a real vacancy.
S3.quote: A certificate cannot replace watching the ground move.
fieldNote: She calculates **2034 robot arrival** against her age and the value of two decades at the mine.
Her **training and job move** depend on mine funding, a place and a posted vacancy; she keeps leading otherwise.

steps.text: Enroll in inspection certification next year if the mine funds a place
Apply for a posted site-safety vacancy after thinking AI arrives

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that a decade to thinking AI in 2036 and robots around 2039 is time to settle the rules together. I would ask the company to keep experienced operators in the safety decisions even if fewer people drive.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 56 when capable robots arrive, and the mortgage should be much smaller if our income holds. I could afford to step back from shifts then, but I don't want the mine to discard practical knowledge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep contributing to our mortgage and retirement savings at the present rate and bring a proposal for operator seats on equipment trials to the union this year. In the first year after thinking AI arrives, I'll compare my pension estimate with a paid safety-adviser vacancy before choosing fewer shifts.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel calm about our household with that much time. I feel less calm about a company deciding that a long record of safe work has no use.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you leave your lead wage for a safety title?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If a safety adviser post pays enough and exists, I'd apply; otherwise I'd keep my lead shifts while they're offered. I won't leave a good wage for a title on a slide.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would your children hear about this plan?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell our children to finish their schooling without asking them to solve my job problem. Their path should be theirs, even while we plan for ours.

say: I would use the **decade** to agree on equipment rules before capable mine robots arrive around 2039.
I would keep **experienced operators** in safety decisions even if fewer people drive.
think: I think at **56**, I may choose fewer shifts if our income holds and the mortgage falls.
I want practical **safety knowledge** to remain useful after mine equipment changes.
do: **Keep paying** into mortgage and retirement savings at our current rate.
**Propose operator seats** on equipment trials this year and compare a paid adviser vacancy with my pension estimate after 2036.
feel: **Calm** about household finances, though worried that safe-work experience may be dismissed.
S4.quote: I won't leave a good wage for a title on a slide.
fieldNote: Her **2039 age** is 56, making reduced shifts a possible choice if household income and mortgage plans hold.
She links **collective voice** on trials with a conditional adviser application, not a guaranteed new role.

steps.text: Keep current mortgage and retirement contributions
Propose operator seats on equipment trials through the union
Compare pension figures with a paid adviser vacancy after 2036

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most for apprentices who have hardly begun earning, even if my own savings give me room. A funded training place at full wages, with selection rules negotiated by the union, would help the crew plan.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who gets heard when new equipment is tested. A safety rule written without drivers is only paper on a wall. I would want the least experienced driver at the table as well as the lead, because that person meets confusing instructions first.

headlineQuote: A safety rule written without drivers is only paper on a wall.
portrait: **Grace Costa**, 43, leads loading work at a large copper mine and has a two-year technical diploma.
Her **high wage** and nine months of savings support a mortgage and two children alongside her partner’s school income.
She tries **AI occasionally** after others prove its use, while insisting that software routes answer to the ground and the drivers.
Her **union work** seeks paid transition places and operator seats on equipment trials, especially for younger workers.
She would **study inspection** only with a funded place and full wages, then apply if a real vacancy opens.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because apprentices lack her savings before capable robots may reach mine equipment around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A **funded training place** at full wages and negotiated selection rules would help the crew plan.
